description: We bring together creativity, technical thinking and collaborative problem-solving to transform ambitious ideas into meaningful solutions. Our mission is not just to explore possibilities but to inspire the next generation to reach for the stars.
summary:
Ask most kids what astronauts do and they’ll say “walk on the Moon.” Ask what keeps those astronauts alive and you’ll get a blank stare. Moon Base Keeper changes that.

In this free browser game, kids aged 7 to 12 run a lunar outpost near the Moon’s south pole for seven days. They build solar panels, air makers and radiation shields, give jobs to a crew of four, and make a call every day. Every choice costs something: shields use power, power makes air, and a solar flare won’t wait until you’re ready.

That flare isn’t made up. Each day’s space weather is based on NASA’s DONKI solar flare data, so the danger on screen comes from real solar activity. There’s nothing to download and no account to create. Just click, build, and find out that in space, nothing is free.
details:
Moon Base Keeper puts a kid in charge of a lunar outpost near the Moon’s south pole for seven days. Each day they check the space weather, build solar panels, air makers and shields, give their four astronauts jobs, and make one big call. Nothing is free: shields use power, power makes air, and a solar flare won’t wait until you’re ready. The flare warning is based on NASA’s DONKI space weather data, so the danger comes from real solar activity.

  • Why it helps: one mission (about 5 to 8 minutes) teaches that a space base is a balancing act. It’s free, runs in any browser, and needs no download or account, so a class can start from a link.
  • Impact we hope for: kids leave knowing that no one gets a free choice in space, and that astronauts are people solving hard problems, which might make them ask, “How would I solve that?”
  • What we used: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, hosted on Netlify with code on GitHub. We wrote it in the Antigravity editor with AI assistance (including Claude) and made the artwork ourselves. Data comes from NASA DONKI, plus facts inspired by NASA’s Open Science Data Repository.
  • What’s creative: the lesson is the game. Every choice has a visible cost, there’s no safe option, and real flare data drives the risk. Each astronaut has a job explained in kid-friendly words, and the game labels what’s real, simplified or fictional.
  • What we considered: ages 7 to 12 get overwhelmed, so we kept the main stats to three and unlocked extra buildings later. We used plain language, favoured accuracy over flashy looks, and made it easy to reach. The numbers are simplified, the 7-day plan is illustrative, and the crew are fictional.
